newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Welcome to rebel-held Congo, not Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Welcome to rebel-held Congo, not Zaire.

text.p: After a mere 25 years of existence, the central African country called Zaire is heading inexorably for the dustbin of history.

Laurent Kabila's apparently unstoppable rebels are not solely intent on toppling President Mobutu Sese Seko. They are also determined to erase the name he gave to Africa's third- largest country in 1972.

Zaire has already become the "Democratic Republic of Congo" in rebel-held territory. Kabila controls nearly half the country and his aides expect to be in the capital, Kinshasa, by June at the latest.

For the next few weeks at least, the mighty river flowing past Kinshasa will still be called the Zaire. Further upstream, when it crosses areas "liberated" by the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), it has become the Congo.
Mobutu re-baptised the currency as well in 1972 when he was at the height of his powers as the West's most coveted Cold War ally in Africa.
The Zaire currency was at par with the dollar 25 years ago. Today it is pitifully weak, exchanging at 75,000 for one U.S. dollar in rebel areas, and is also on the way out.

"After we have liberated the whole country we are going to launch our own currency and call it the Congolese Franc," said Walle Lufungula, a lawyer aged 32 who has just been appointed head of the Alliance in the province once called Haut-Zaire.
Now it has reverted to its pre-Mobutu name of Eastern province with its capital in Kisangani.
After Kabila's men capture Lubumbashi, the mineral-rich province of which it is the capital will revert to the name Katanga and stop being Shaba.

All the new names, including the Democratic Republic of Congo, are actually old. They go back to the period after the country's independence from Belgium in 1960 and before Mobutu's military coup in 1965.
"The idea is to return to the pre-Mobutu names. He had no need to change them," Walle said in an interview.

Mobutu's motives for the rash of altered nomenclature in 1972 were complex. They fitted in with his drive for "authenticity", a doggerel philosophy which eschewed European garments and outlawed Christian first names in favour of African ones.

"If you wore a tie in public you could be arrested and if you called a friend by his Christian name you ran a risk," Professor Ndomba Benda, a professor of linguistics at Kisangani University, told Reuters.

"But the changes were all superficial. There was no substance and behind the facade there was a dustbin," said the highly trained academic whose salary today, at the age of 51, is less than $30 a month.

Even the word Zaire was a mispronunciation by Portuguese explorers in the 15th century. When they arrived from the Atlantic at the estuary of the great river now called the Zaire or the Congo, the local Kongo tribe told them it was a Nzadi, meaning river.
"So the choice of the word Zaire was an example of Mobutu's own cultural alienation which he then disguised as authenticity," Ndomba said.
For many in the Alliance, their political reference is Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister after independence and a symbol of liberation throughout Africa.

He was captured in Kisangani and assassinated early in 1961, his name entering political oblivion in the Mobutu era. If and when Kabila becomes master of the whole country, Lumumba will be restored to glory.
"We want to start again from the period of Patrice Lumumba, who is our national hero," said the Alliance's Walle.
